legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Variational Inference: A Review for Statisticians", David M. Blei, Alp Kucukelbir, Jon D. McAuliffe.
Venue as printed: preprint only. The PDF prints "arXiv:1601.00670v9 [stat.CO] 9 May 2018" and a title-page date of "May 11, 2018". No journal name, volume or acceptance note appears. The only "American Statistical" hits are reference entries for other papers. The filename's 2016 is not printed in the PDF except through the 1601 arXiv id. Any journal citation needs another source.

COVERAGE: 114,117 of 114,117 chars, all 41 pages, none empty. References were read for origins. Pages 9 and 17 were also rendered to check extraction and read Figure 6. Nothing was skipped.

CLAIMS

VI vs MCMC

- claim: MCMC is asymptotically exact but heavier. VI only finds a nearby density but tends to be faster.
  number: none
  setup: general guidance, not a measured result
  quote: "MCMC methods tend to be more computationally intensive than variational inference but they also provide guarantees of producing (asymptotically) exact samples from the target density (Robert and Casella, 2004). Variational inference does not enjoy such guarantees—it can only ﬁnd a density close to the target—but tends to be faster than MCMC ."
  where: p3

- claim: Use VI for large data and fast model exploration. Use MCMC for small data where precision justifies the cost.
  number: 20 years; one billion documents (both are illustrative scenarios, not experiments)
  setup: authors' hypothetical examples
  quote: "we might use MCMC in a setting where we spent 20 years collecting a small but expensive data set, where we are conﬁdent that our model is appropriate, and where we require precise inferences. We might use variational inference when ﬁtting a probabilistic model of text to one billion text documents"
  where: p3

- claim: Posterior geometry also matters. For mixtures where Gibbs is unavailable, VI may beat HMC even on small data.
  number: none
  setup: multimodal mixture posteriors, citing Kucukelbir et al. 2015
  quote: "For mixture models where Gibbs sampling is not an option, variational inference may perform better than a more general MCMC technique (e.g., Hamiltonian Monte Carlo), even for small datasets (Kucukelbir et al., 2015)."
  where: p3

- claim: Relative accuracy is unresolved. VI underestimates variance generally, yet predictive accuracy need not suffer.
  number: none
  setup: review of empirical lines of work
  quote: "The relative accuracy of variational inference and MCMC is still unknown. We do know that variational inference generally underestimates the variance of the posterior density; this is a consequence of its objective function."
  where: p3
  second quote: "variational inference does not necessarily suffer in accuracy, e.g., in terms of posterior predictive densities" (p3)

KL direction and variance

- claim: KL(q||p) penalises q placing mass where p has little, and penalises the reverse less, so marginals come out too narrow.
  number: none
  setup: illustrated on a highly correlated 2D Gaussian posterior under mean-field. The approximation has the same mean as the target. The authors call the effect common, not universal.
  quote: "It penalizes placing mass in q(·) on areas where p(·) has little mass, but penalizes less the reverse. In this example, in order to successfully match the marginal variances, the circular q(·) would have to expand into territory where p(·) has little mass."
  where: p9

- claim: For Bayesian Gaussian mixtures, the asymptotic variational covariance is provably too small.
  number: O(1/n) is the rate at which the VI estimate and MLE approach each other
  setup: Wang and Titterington 2005, 2006: conjugate priors, mean-field, variational posterior mean as estimator
  quote: "the VI estimate and maximum likelihood estimate (MLE) approach each other at a rate ofO (1/n). In Wang and Titterington (2005), they show that the asymptotic variational posterior covariance matrix is “too small”—it differs from the MLE covariance (i.e., the inverse Fisher information) by a positive-deﬁnite matrix."
  where: p25

ELBO

- claim: The KL is not computable because it contains log p(x), so VI maximises the ELBO, which is equivalent up to a constant.
  number: none (equations 12-14)
  setup: any model and any q
  quote: "ELBO (q) = E [log p(z,x)]− E [log q(z)] . (13)"
  where: p6
  second quote: "log p(x) = KL (q(z)‖p(z|x)) + ELBO (q). (14)" (p7)

- claim: The ELBO balances expected likelihood against closeness to the prior.
  number: none
  setup: general
  quote: "= E [log p(x|z)]− KL (q(z)‖p(z)) ."
  where: p6

- claim: Picking a model by its ELBO sometimes works but has no theoretical justification.
  number: none
  setup: model selection
  quote: "Though this sometimes works in practice, selecting based on a bound is not justiﬁed in theory."
  where: p7

Mean-field

- claim: Mean-field makes all latent variables independent. It can capture any marginal but no correlation.
  number: none
  setup: equation 15, q(z) = product of q_j(z_j). The family is not a model of the data.
  quote: "it can capture any marginal density of the latent variables. However, it cannot capture correlation between them."
  where: p8

- claim: The independence assumption helps scaling but can worsen local optima and variance underestimation.
  number: none
  setup: stated as an open problem
  quote: "they can exacerbate issues with local optima of the objective and underestimating posterior variances; see Figure 1."
  where: p26

CAVI

- claim: CAVI updates each factor in turn from the expected log complete conditional, the same conditional Gibbs samples from.
  number: none (equations 17-18)
  setup: mean-field family
  quote: "The Gibbs sampler main-tains a realization of the latent variables and iteratively samples from each variable’s com-plete conditional. Equation (18) uses the same complete conditional." (the hyphen breaks and the join across the Figure 1 stale-text boundary were normalised, see PROBLEMS; the sentence itself is on p10)
  where: p10

- claim: CAVI reaches only a local optimum, and the outcome depends on initialisation.
  number: 10 random initialisations, each reaching a different value
  setup: Gaussian mixture on the image data
  quote: "Figure 2 shows the ELBO trajectory for 10 random initializations using the Gaussian mixture model."
  where: p11
  second quote: "CAVI only guar-antees convergence to a local optimum" (p11, line break as extracted)

- claim: Landing in one label-switching mode is often sufficient for mixtures.
  number: none
  setup: when the goal is exploring clusters or predicting new observations
  quote: "Representing one of these modes is sufﬁcient for exploring latent clusters or predicting new observations."
  where: p11

- claim: Exact evidence for a mixture is intractable.
  number: K^n configurations
  setup: Bayesian mixture of unit-variance Gaussians
  quote: "The time complexity of numerically evaluating the K-dimensional integral isO (K n)."
  where: pp5-6 (superscript lost in extraction)

Empirical examples

- claim: CAVI fits a 30-cluster GMM to 10,000 images in under a minute and is orders of magnitude faster than Stan's HMC sampler.
  number: 30 clusters; 576 dimensions; 10,000 training and 10,000 test images; under a minute. No speed ratio or hardware is stated.
  setup: imageCLEF colour histograms, compared on held-out average log predictive. Details are in Appendix B: diagonal-covariance GMM, a0 = 1/K, Stan with assignments marginalised out.
  quote: "We use CAVI to ﬁt a Gaussian mixture model with thirty clusters to image histograms. We randomly select two sets of ten thousand images from the imageCLEF collection to serve as training and testing datasets." and "CAVI is orders of magnitude faster than this sampling algorithm."
  second quote: "concatenating the three color histograms gives a 576-dimensional representation" (p16)
  third quote: "CAVI ﬁts a Gaussian mixture model to ten thousand images in less than a minute." (p17, Figure 6 caption)
  where: p16

- claim: The authors say this comparison does not settle VI vs MCMC.
  number: none
  setup: footnote 5
  quote: "This is not a deﬁnitive comparison between variational inference and MCMC . Other samplers, such as a collapsed Gibbs sampler, may perform better than Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampling."
  where: p16

- claim: The simulation study shows ELBO "elbows" on a non-convex objective.
  number: K = 5
  setup: 2D data, simulated Gaussians with random means and covariances. Sample size is not stated.
  quote: "We simulate K = 5 Gaussians with random means, covariances, and mixture assignments."
  where: p14

SVI

- claim: CAVI iterates over all the data each round. SVI subsamples, using a noisy unbiased natural gradient.
  number: none
  setup: conditionally conjugate models, optimising global parameters. Reaches a local optimum.
  quote: "The noisy natural gradient ˆg(λ) is unbiased: Et [ˆg(λ)] = g(λ). And it is cheap to compute— it only involves a single sampled data point and only one set of optimized local parameters."
  where: p21

- claim: Step sizes must satisfy the Robbins-Monro conditions.
  number: κ in (0.5, 1]
  setup: step-size schedule
  quote: "Many sequences will satisfy these conditions, for exampleεt = t−κ forκ∈ (0.5, 1]."
  where: p21

- claim: SVI needs no new derivation beyond CAVI.
  number: none
  setup: conditionally conjugate models
  quote: "We emphasize that SVI requires no new derivation beyond what is needed for CAVI."
  where: p21

- claim: SVI took topic models from thousands of documents to millions.
  number: 1.8M articles. No timing is given.
  setup: LDA on the New York Times, reproduced from Hoffman et al. 2013
  quote: "Figure 7 illustrates topics inferred using the latent Dirichlet allocation model (Blei et al., 2003) from 1.8M articles from the New York Times. This analysis would not have been possible without SVI."
  where: p22

Practicalities

- claim: Held-out log predictive is a cheaper convergence proxy than the full ELBO, but it is not monotone.
  number: none
  setup: CAVI monitoring
  quote: "Unlike the full ELBO , held-out predictive probability is not guaranteed to monotonically increase across iterations of CAVI."
  where: p11

- claim: Non-conjugate models such as Bayesian logistic regression fall outside the basic recipe. Black-box and automatic methods address them.
  number: none
  setup: section 5.3, including ADVI in Stan, which the authors call a step towards derivation-free VI
  quote: "The posterior density of the coefﬁcients is not in an exponential family and we cannot apply the variational inference methods we discussed above."
  where: p25

- claim: Footnote 1 treats the Laplace approximation as variational in the broad sense. The review itself covers KL(q||p).
  number: none
  setup: definition, per Wainwright and Jordan 2008
  quote: "This includes methods like expectation propagation (Minka, 2001), belief propagation (Yedidia et al., 2001), or even the Laplace approximation."
  where: p3

Open problems (pp24-26)

- Alternative divergences, such as α-divergence and EP's "other direction". These "may be difﬁcult to optimize" but "may give better approximations" (p26).
- Richer families with efficient optimisation: structured VI, non-diagonal Gaussians, Giordano et al.'s variance correction, hierarchical variational models (p26).
- Combining VI and MCMC: "A principled analysis of when to use (and combine) variational inference and MCMC would have both theoretical and practical impact in the ﬁeld." (p26)
- VI as an estimator: "the statistical properties of variational inference are not yet well understood, espe-cially in contrast to the wealth of analysis ofMCMC techniques." (p26)

LIMITS

- No exactness guarantee and no general accuracy bound. Bounding theory is something the authors only "envision" (p4).
- Theory is piecemeal: "Each result revolves around a single model and a single family of variational approximations." (p24) Results treat VI posterior means as point estimates, and "Sometimes the research ﬁnds that they do not enjoy the same asymptotics." (p24)
- The image study reports speed and held-out predictive only. It does not compare posterior variances or intervals against MCMC, so it does not measure the variance problem. It is one model, one sampler, no stated hardware, and no prose NUTS timing.
- VI's convergence is to a local optimum, and the ELBO does not tell you how far q is from p. The paper offers no diagnostic of approximation quality.
- Focus is mean-field and conditionally conjugate models.
- Dated: the arXiv version is from 2018, but its citations stop at 2016 and the Stan reference is 2.8.0. The review does not mention normalizing flows or any later VI quality diagnostic. The "VI is faster" guidance predates current samplers and hardware, and the PDF cannot speak to them.

BUILDS ON (as printed)

- MCMC: Metropolis et al. 1953; Hastings 1970; Geman and Geman 1984; Gelfand and Smith 1990.
- Early VI, two tracks: Peterson and Anderson 1987 ("arguably the ﬁrst variational procedure", Complex Systems), with Parisi 1988, Saul et al. 1996, Jaakkola and Jordan 1996/1997, Ghahramani and Jordan 1997, and Jordan et al. 1999 (Machine Learning). Second track: Hinton and Van Camp 1993 (Computational Learning Theory), Neal and Hinton 1999 ("ﬁrst published in 1993"), MacKay 1997, Waterhouse et al. 1996.
- EM: Dempster et al. 1977 (JRSS B). KL: Kullback and Leibler 1951 (Annals of Mathematical Statistics).
- CAVI: Bishop 2006. Message passing: Winn and Bishop 2005 (JMLR).
- SVI: Hoffman et al. 2013 (JMLR); Robbins and Monro 1951 (Annals of Mathematical Statistics); Amari 1982, 1998.
- Survey anchor: Wainwright and Jordan 2008.
- Black-box and automatic VI: Ranganath et al. 2014; Kingma and Welling 2014 (ICLR); Rezende et al. 2014 (ICML); Kucukelbir et al. 2015 (NeurIPS, printed as "Neural Information Processing Systems") and 2016 (arXiv).
- NUTS: Hoffman and Gelman 2014 (JMLR). This is also the source the target note already cites.

CODE

- Log-sum-exp identity, p11, equation 20: log sum exp(x_i) = α + log sum exp(x_i − α), with α "typically set to maxi xi".
- Stan GMM, p30, Figure 8. The extraction is letter-spaced and should be re-read from the page. Its point is stated on p29: "Since Stan does not support discrete latent variables, we marginalize over the assignment variables." Algorithms 1 (p10), 2 (p14) and 3 (p23) are compact pseudocode.

FIGURES

- Figure 1, p9: "Visualizing the mean-ﬁeld approximation to a two-dimensional Gaussian posterior. The ellipses show the effect of mean-ﬁeld factorization." A round q sits inside an elongated p, which shows lost correlation and shrunken marginals at a glance. Best candidate.
- Figure 6, p17: "Comparison of CAVI to a Hamiltonian Monte Carlo-based sampling technique." Shows the speed gap and the metric on one axis. My reading of the rendered plot, approximate and not stated in the text: CAVI reaches about 0 within a few seconds and stays flat. NUTS starts near -1000 at about 15-20 s and reaches about -500 by about 140 s, then stays there to about 260 s. Do not cite these readings as reported values.
- Figure 2, p11: "Different initializations may lead CAVI to ﬁnd different local optima of the ELBO." Shows multiple ELBO trajectories over 0-50 seconds. Explains local optima faster than prose.
- Figure 3, p15: "A simulation study of a two dimensional Gaussian mixture model." Shows ELBO elbows alongside fitted components by iteration.
- Figure 7, p22: 1.8M NYT topics. Useful for scale only.
- Figures 4, 5 and 8 (pp16, 17, 30) support the image example and add little beyond it.

PROBLEMS

- Stale hidden text on p9: the Figure 1 image embeds an older draft of section 2.4, so extraction emits duplicate text ("distribution" where the final says "density"), garbled equations, and page marker "9". Rendering confirms this text is not visible on the page. Quotes above use the visible version.
- Figure 3's embedded plot also extracts a stray "Figure 1: Main caption" (p15). It is not visible content that matters.
- Equations partly garbled by extraction (superscripts lost, as in O(K n)). Figure 8 code is letter-spaced. Ligatures and hyphen breaks are kept in quotes except where noted.
- Oddities in the source itself, as printed:
  - p6 says computing the evidence is "exponential in K", although the count given is K^n, which is exponential in n.
  - The Figure 6 legend says "NUTS (Hoﬀman et al. 2013)", while the text cites Hoffman and Gelman (2014).
  - Algorithm 3's update prints λt on both sides and uses f(zt, xt), whereas equation 54 uses λt−1 and the text uses t(·,·).
- No embedded instructions found.
